rationale: The sources define a centred power series and its radius and interval of convergence. The item adds an extended-real supremum construction, an explicit empty-set convention, and repository indexing conventions, so it is a semantic adaptation.

The sources give the Cauchy–Hadamard reciprocal formula with the zero, finite-positive, and infinite limit-superior cases. The item shifts the root sequence to zero-based indexing and works only over the reals; its proof adapts the standard root-test argument.

The sources state absolute convergence strictly inside the radius, divergence outside, and unconstrained endpoint behaviour. The item packages those clauses as a real, convention-complete corollary and proves them from its local Cauchy–Hadamard theorem.

The sources state compact-subset uniform convergence inside the convergence disc or interval. The item specializes this to closed real subintervals with explicit endpoint inequalities and supplies an M-test proof.

The literature states that a power-series sum is continuous, indeed analytic, in the interior of its convergence interval. The item derives the real statement through local uniform convergence and polynomial partial sums.

The sources state termwise differentiation and integration without changing the radius. The item isolates a bespoke three-series comparison lemma and gives its own coefficient-bound proof, so the statement is a semantic extraction and the proof is locally generated.

The sources state termwise differentiation throughout the open convergence interval with the same radius. The item expresses coefficients through canonical naturals and adapts the proof to the library's uniform-derivative theorem.

The sources give termwise antiderivatives and integration of power series inside the radius. The item adds a closed-subinterval integral identity and zero-constant-term normalization, with a proof adapted through the local FTC and uniform integration theorem.

The sources state infinite differentiability and the coefficient formula a_n=f^(n)(c)/n!. The item expands all iterates using falling factorials and canonical embeddings, so the statement and induction proof are semantic adaptations.

The sources explain recentering a power series by binomial expansion and absolute rearrangement. The item isolates the exact double-series convergence region |d-c|+|h|<R and proves the bookkeeping locally.

The sources state that a power-series sum re-expands about each interior point and that the new coefficients are its Taylor coefficients. The item supplies the explicit real radius R-|d-c| and adapts the proof through its double-series lemma.

The sources define real analyticity by a locally convergent power-series representation. The item makes the open-domain and neighbourhood quantifiers explicit in repository notation, a semantic notational adaptation.
The sources state that a power-series sum is analytic throughout the interior of its convergence interval. The item derives the claim from its explicit interior recentering theorem.
The sources state that real-analytic functions are infinitely differentiable. The item proves the local-to-global real statement using the library's coefficient formula.

The literature gives the standard zero alternative obtained from the first nonzero Taylor coefficient. The item phrases it for real-analytic functions with a local-neighbourhood conclusion and expands the conventional proof.

The sources give uniqueness or identity theorems for analytic functions from an accumulating zero set. The item specializes to an open real interval and propagates local vanishing by connectedness, so it is semantically sourced.

The sources give multiplication of convergent power series by coefficient convolution. The item states the real common-radius version and adapts the proof through the library's absolute Cauchy-product theorem.
The sources state local substitution or composition of convergent power series. The item adds the sufficient majorant B_r<S and a double-series regrouping proof, so both components are adapted.
The sources state that a power series with nonzero constant term has a locally convergent reciprocal series. The item uses a geometric-series majorant and locally generated regrouping details.

The sources state closure of analytic functions under sums, products, nonvanishing quotients, and composition. The item consolidates these with explicit compatible-domain hypotheses and a proof through its local series lemmas.

The sources define Abel summability through a radial power-series limit and Cesàro summability through arithmetic means of partial sums. The item combines both under zero-based inclusive conventions, so it is a semantic adaptation.

The sources state Abel's limit theorem for a convergent zero-indexed series with the same radial limit at one. The item follows the standard Abel-summation proof but expands convergence of the Abel series and all endpoint quantifiers.

The literature records the generating-function relation behind Cesàro and Abel methods. The item isolates the exact zero-indexed transform with weights (n+1)(1-x)^2 and proves the algebra and convergence locally.
The sources state that Cesàro (C,1) summability implies Abel summability to the same value. The item gives the zero-indexed weighted-kernel formulation and adapts the classical proof.
The sources state regularity of Cesàro and Abel summation: ordinary convergence is preserved with the same sum. The item packages both consequences in the library's definitions.

The source states Tauber's condition a_n=o(1/n) and its convergence consequence. The displayed block and weighted estimates are a bespoke elementary lemma extracted for the local proof, with a locally generated derivation.

The source states Tauber's converse: Abel summability plus a_n=o(1/n) implies ordinary convergence to the Abel sum. The item uses the equivalent shifted condition (n+1)a_n→0 and adapts the standard x_N=1-1/(N+1) proof.

The source states uniform convergence on compact subsets rather than on the whole open interval. The item formulates the stronger false claim and refutes it with the geometric series by an explicit local computation.

The source states radial convergence only inside the distance of a known convergence point and permits divergence farther out. The item turns the overstatement into a false statement and gives the geometric-series counterexample locally.

The sources explain that Abel summability alone need not imply ordinary convergence and use divergent Abel-summable examples. The item formulates the false converse and refutes it with Grandi's series.
The sources give the geometric series and interior recentering of power-series sums. The item combines them into the explicit coefficient formula about an arbitrary real c and verifies it directly.

The sources state that endpoint behaviour is independent of the common radius and exhibit standard endpoint alternatives. The item's selected p-series and alternating-harmonic trio is a locally worked construction.
The Encyclopedia explicitly gives Σ n!(z-a)^n as a radius-zero example. The item is its real specialization, while the coefficient-root verification is written locally.

The source limits uniform convergence to compact subsets inside the radius. The item supplies the standard geometric-series counterexample on the entire open interval and a local uniform-Cauchy refutation.
The sources derive rational-function analyticity from geometric or reciprocal power series. The item works out the local series of 1/(2-x) at an arbitrary c≠2.
The sources state Abel's theorem and discuss the alternating harmonic series as an application. The item records the zero-indexed version and applies the local theorem directly.
The source explicitly treats Grandi's divergent series and its Abel value 1/2. The item gives the same construction in the library's zero-indexed notation with a local calculation.

The sources develop Abel and Cesàro summability and the Cauchy-product generating-function calculation. The item works out the classical 1-2+3-4+… separation example and its two Cesàro subsequences locally.
The source defines axis-parallel closed rectangles in R^n and their product volume. The item adds explicit nondegenerate and degenerate conventions in finite-index notation.
The source defines partitions of rectangles into coordinate cells. The item packages coordinatewise grids, cell indexing, mesh, refinement, and exact volume splitting in repository notation.
The source defines multidimensional lower and upper Darboux sums over rectangular partitions. The item uses grid-cell extrema and iterated finite sums with explicit boundedness conventions.
The source gives refinement monotonicity for multidimensional Darboux sums. The item's additional boundary-slab estimate with a fixed-grid constant is a bespoke bridge proved locally.
The source defines lower and upper multidimensional integrals as extrema of Darboux sums and integrability by equality. The item adapts this to its grid conventions and nondegenerate rectangles.
The source gives the Darboux small-gap criterion in several variables. The item states it for the local grid definitions and adapts the common-refinement proof.
The literature uses tagged rectangular partitions and mesh-controlled Riemann sums. The item makes the coordinate-grid and universal-tag quantifiers explicit.

The standard literature equates Darboux integrability with the universal small-mesh tagged-sum criterion. The item adapts this to coordinate grids and supplies boundary-slab and finite-choice details.
The source's one- and several-variable definitions coincide under R^1≅R. The item isolates that dictionary as a convention bridge and verifies each component directly.

The source states linearity, order preservation, absolute-value control, and rectangular additivity for the multidimensional Riemann integral. The item consolidates these and adapts the Darboux-grid proof.

The source proves that a continuous function on a closed rectangle is Riemann integrable by compactness and uniform continuity. The item translates the proof through the Euclidean/sup-norm comparison.

The source defines measure-zero covers and finite content-zero covers using rectangles or balls. The item standardizes on closed cubes and distinguishes countable nullity from finite content zero, so conventions differ.
The source definitions reduce to interval covers in one dimension. The item records the exact dictionary with the library's earlier one-dimensional definitions.
The source states subset closure and countable-union closure for null sets. The item exposes the countable-choice and N²-enumeration commitments and adapts the usual epsilon-budget proof.

The source states that compact null sets admit finite arbitrarily small covers. Combined with the immediate converse, this is the item's equivalence under cube-cover conventions; the proof adapts compactness and padding.
The source defines point oscillation in R^n using relative balls and shrinking radii. The item uses extended suprema and an explicit empty-set convention, a semantic adaptation.
The source states continuity iff point oscillation is zero and closedness of positive oscillation superlevels. The item proves the same result under its extended-real oscillation convention.

The sources convert small rectangle covers to partition control in the standard Lebesgue-criterion proof. The item isolates a quantified finite-cover-to-grid lemma with arbitrary excess η and proves it constructively.

The source states the multidimensional Lebesgue–Vitali criterion for bounded functions on closed rectangles. The item replaces outer measure by its cube-cover nullity definition and expands both directions, so the conventions are semantically rather than textually identical.

The source defines Jordan measurability through indicator integrability and volume. The item instead begins with finite rectangle-cover infima and disjoint inscribed suprema and then defines equality, an equivalent but different construction.

The source defines Jordan measurability by integrability of the global characteristic function and identifies its integral with volume. The item proves equivalence with its inner/outer-content construction on a bounding rectangle.

Lebl Proposition 10.5.1 exactly supports that a bounded subset of R^n is Jordan measurable iff its ambient boundary is null. The added equivalence with content zero and the relative-domain indicator proof on an enlarged rectangle are local adaptations licensed by the internal compact-null/content-zero lemma and the cited boundary, compactness, and integrability interfaces.

The source defines integration over a Jordan set by zero extension to a containing rectangle and states rectangle independence. The item adopts that construction with explicit boundedness and empty-set conventions.
The source states independence of the containing rectangle. The item isolates it as a lemma and supplies locally generated coordinate-slice and null-face bookkeeping.
The source states integrability of bounded continuous functions on bounded Jordan sets. The item uses compactness to obtain boundedness and adapts the zero-extension discontinuity proof.
The source states finite additivity of Jordan volume. The item strengthens the two-set hypothesis to allow content-zero overlap and derives the disjoint-family clause by induction.
The source proves null-set preservation under locally Lipschitz control arising from bounded derivatives. The item extracts the equal-dimensional global Lipschitz case and uses cube scaling directly.

The source states that the graph of an integrable, hence continuous-on-a-rectangle, function has Jordan measure zero. The item states the continuous rectangular-domain case in R^(m+1) and gives a direct stack-of-cubes proof.

The literature supplies the section or slicing intuition behind product-volume lower bounds. The item's exact finite-cover inequality for A×[0,d] is a bespoke elementary bridge with a locally generated strip proof.

This is a positive AI-invention determination: the remark is an item-by-item account of this library's chosen rectangle, nullity, image-theorem, and integration scope. That repository-specific dependency ledger has no external mathematical statement counterpart; each mathematical scope assertion was checked against the named on-disk item.
The source explicitly gives the integral of a constant over a rectangle as c times its volume. The unit-box specialization and coordinate-product verification are worked locally.

The Utah notes explicitly use the rational points of the unit square as a non-Jordan set whose boundary is the whole square; the nullity source covers countable rational points. The item combines those standard facts in its local conventions.
The sources give a compact nowhere-dense fat Cantor set of positive size and the Jordan boundary criterion. The item's slab S×[0,1] construction and product lower-bound proof are locally assembled.

The sources give fat Cantor sets and standard bounded open non-Jordan examples. The item uses the specific complement-times-interval construction and proves its boundary contains a positive-content slab.
The source states that graphs of continuous functions on Jordan rectangles have zero Jordan measure. The item specializes to x↦x² on [0,1] and applies the local graph theorem.

The sources establish Jordan measurability of regions bounded by continuous graphs and identify Jordan volume by indicator integration. The item's exact N-by-N cell count for the standard triangle is a locally generated computation.

The sources give content zero for the ordinary Cantor set and the product/Jordan-cover framework. The item constructs explicit square stacks over a finite interval cover and contrasts them with the fat-Cantor slab.

Munkres explicitly calls a bounded set rectifiable when its indicator is integrable, proves equivalence with null boundary, and explains that the term is borrowed from curve-length terminology. The item faithfully records that convention and disambiguation.
